chunk_findings.detail: The registered schema declares a `limit` property ("Rows returned, most effort first (default 25; 0 = all)."), but the api lambda is `lambda repo, a, agent: _api().progress(repo, a.get("id", "") or "")` — it never forwards `a["limit"]`. Every other tool in this registry forwards each declared property to its `_api()` call (cf. `ddflow_dupes` passing `limit=int(a.get("limit") or 0)`, `ddflow_recall` passing `limit=int(a.get("limit") or 3)`, `ddflow_onboard` passing every declared arg). Consequently, calling `ddflow_progress` with `limit=0` (documented as "all") or `limit=5` has no effect: the argument is silently discarded, so the caller gets a different number of rows than the tool's own schema promises. If the pre-move lambda forwarded `limit`, this is a behaviour change introduced by the move; if the schema is authoritative, the documented `0 = all` / default-25 contract is unenforceable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/tools/reporting.py:ddflow_progress

chunk_findings.detail: The moved `_AGENT_KEYS` is a verbatim copy of the version deleted from `ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py`, and its body contains `from ..services.adopt import AGENT_TARGETS`. That import is *inside the function*, not in the module header, and the docstring even advertises this ("The import is inside the function only to keep it out of this module's header"). A mechanical "deepen every header import one level" pass therefore misses it. In the new location `ddflow/surfaces/tools/_common.py`, `..` resolves to `ddflow.surfaces`, so `..services.adopt` becomes `ddflow.surfaces.services.adopt`, which does not exist — it must be `...services.adopt` (`ddflow.services.adopt`). Because `_AGENT_KEYS()` is *called at registry-build time* to render `ddflow_setup`'s `agents` property (`f"{','.join(_AGENT_KEYS())}. Default: all."`), the failure is not latent: importing `ddflow.surfaces.tools` — and thus `import ddflow.surfaces.mcp`, which now does `from .tools import TOOLS` at module top — raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'ddflow.surfaces.services'` before `TOOLS` is ever populated. Every test or caller that imports `ddflow.surfaces.mcp` (the very compatibility surface this refactor claims to preserve) breaks. The fix is to change the in-body import to `from ...services.adopt import AGENT_TARGETS`.

chunk_findings.detail: The removed loop is an import-time side effect that mutates the shared `TOOLS` registry; it is not a binding, so re-exporting `ADD_TOOLS` and `DEDUPE_PROPERTIES` (or importing the slices) does not reproduce it. In the original module the loop provably runs after the whole `TOOLS` dict exists in the same namespace. After the move, `TOOLS` is assembled in `tools/__init__.py` from per-slice dicts, so the loop only has the intended effect if it is executed against the *same* objects that end up in the exported registry. If `tools/__init__.py` builds the registry by copying the slice dicts (e.g. `TOOLS = {**lifecycle.TOOLS, **flow.TOOLS, ...}` after the slice modules are imported and run their own copy of the loop), or if a slice runs the loop before the add-tool entries are merged, the in-place `properties.update(DEDUPE_PROPERTIES)` lands on entries that are not the ones `tools/list` later advertises. Concrete result: `ddflow_phase_add`, `ddflow_task_add`, `ddflow_bug_found`, `ddflow_lesson_add`, `ddflow_decision_add`, `ddflow_research_add`, `ddflow_memory_add` are advertised without the `relation` and `check_only` properties — the duplicate-check workflow documented by `_answer` becomes unreachable to a client that relies on the schema, even though `TOOLS` "content" otherwise looks unchanged. The move list in the intent ("TOOLS dict, helpers, tier sets") never mentions this executable statement, so it is the one piece of this hunk whose placement determines behaviour.

chunk_findings.detail: The lambda maps both an omitted `limit` and an explicit `limit` of `0` to `None`: `int(a["limit"]) if a.get("limit") else None`. For the documented input `{"limit": 0}`, `a.get("limit")` is the integer `0`, which is falsy, so the expression yields `None` rather than `0`. The downstream `decision_list` call therefore takes the default path (25 newest decisions) instead of the documented “0 = all” behavior stated in the same tool’s `limit` description: `"Newest decisions returned (default 25; 0 = all)."` Since the MCP property type is `integer`, JSON `0` is the canonical representation that should trigger “all”, and the lambda makes that case unreachable while also being unable to distinguish it from an absent `limit`.

chunk_findings.detail: The registry entry for `ddflow_gate_record` is `("gate", "outcome", "warning")`, and the adjacent B160 comment explicitly states this “ADDS a key to a body consumers already parse” and distinguishes it from the migration. That is a response-contract change for the MCP tool, not a verbatim move: callers that previously received a two-key body now receive a third `warning` key. Concrete failure: an MCP client that unpacks the body as `gate, outcome = result.body` now raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack`, and a strict schema validator expecting only `gate`/`outcome` rejects the response. The stated intent is a pure move, so this payload addition is a behaviour difference.

chunk_findings.detail:
The `ddflow_progress` entry declares a functional `limit` input — `"limit": ("integer", "Rows returned, most effort first (default 25; 0 = all).", False)` — but the lambda drops it entirely:

```python
"api": lambda repo, a, agent: _api().progress(repo, a.get("id", "") or ""),
```

No `limit=` is forwarded, so the caller's value never reaches `progress`. Concrete failure: a caller invoking `ddflow_progress` with `limit=0` (documented as "all") or `limit=10` gets whatever `progress`'s own default is (25 per the description), not the requested count — the declared "0 = all" contract is silently unreachable. Compare the sibling tools in the same file that do forward it (`ddflow_recall`: `limit=int(a.get("limit") or 3)`; `ddflow_dupes`: `limit=int(a.get("limit") or 0)`), which is why this looks like an argument lost in the move rather than intentional. If the original lambda passed a `limit` expression, this is a behaviour difference; if the pre-move code also omitted it, it is a pre-existing dead-parameter bug rather than a refactor regression. Either way the declared input is inert.

chunk_findings.detail:
The tool advertises a `limit` property (`"limit": ("integer", "Maximum results (default 100).", False)`), but the api lambda only forwards `tag` and `scope`:

```python
"api": lambda repo, a, agent: _api().rule_list(
    repo,
    tag=a.get("tag") or None,
    scope=a.get("scope") or None,
),
```

A caller invoking `ddflow_rule_list` with `{"tag": "naming", "limit": 5}` gets the library default (up to 100 rows) instead of 5 — the argument is accepted by the schema and silently discarded. The sibling `ddflow_rule_search` in the same file demonstrates the intended shape (`limit=int(a.get("limit", 10) or 10)`), so this is a dropped pass-through, not a deliberate omission.

chunk_findings.detail:
The tool declares `reason` ("Why it is removed (recorded).") and its description states the removal "is logged as an event", but the lambda drops it:

```python
"api": lambda repo, a, agent: _api().rule_remove(
    repo,
    a["id"],
),
```

With input `{"id": "r-naming", "reason": "superseded by r-naming-v2"}`, the call is made as `rule_remove(repo, "r-naming")`; the reason never reaches the API, so whatever records the removal event cannot record the stated cause, contradicting both the property description and the tool description.

chunk_findings.detail: In `handle`, a notification (no `id`) that carries the modern `_meta` and `method == "server/discover"` reaches the branch `reply = _ok(msg.get("id"), self._discover())` and then `return _modernize(method, reply)`. For a notification `msg.get("id")` is absent/None, so `_ok(None, ...)` still yields a response envelope (with `id: null`/omitted), and that dict is returned from `handle` and written back. This is exactly the case the code's own comment acknowledges one branch earlier ("A refusal can only be ANSWERED to a request; a notification has no id" — handled by `return era if "id" in msg else None`), but the success path never applies that check. Concrete input: `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"server/discover","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}` (no `id`) produces a `server/discover` result instead of silence, so the server replies to a notification. Note this only triggers when `_modern_check` accepts the message as modern (i.e. required `clientCapabilities` is present); a notification lacking it is correctly dropped, which is what makes the omission in the success branch a real, reachable gap rather than dead code.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:handle (server/discover branch)

chunk_findings.detail:
A notification can be turned into a reply. `_modern_check` derives `mid = msg.get("id")` (None for a notification) and then returns `_err(mid, ...)` on two paths — the unsupported-version path and the missing-`clientCapabilities` path — without ever checking whether the message had an `id` at all. Given a modern notification such as

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/cancelled",
 "params":{"requestId":1,
```

A notification can be turned into a reply. `_modern_check` derives `mid = msg.get("id")` (None for a notification) and then returns `_err(mid, ...)` on two paths — the unsupported-version path and the missing-`clientCapabilities` path — without ever checking whether the message had an `id` at all. Given a modern notification such as

```json

 "params":{"requestId":1,
           "_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28"}}}
```

(or any modern notification carrying an unsupported version), `meta` is a dict with `META_VERSION`, the version is in `MODERN_PROTOCOLS`, and `meta.get(META_CLIENT_CAPS)` is not a dict, so the function returns `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":null,"error":{"code":-32602,...}}`. chunk_findings.detail: The removed block registers `_doc` calls in an order that is *not* the dataclass declaration order, so the stated mechanism for preserving `KNOB_DOCS` order (importing section modules "in declaration order") cannot reproduce it. In the deleted text the section sequence is: schedule, bugs, memory, dedupe, importer, companions, **gates (rate_min_runs, rate_max_fail)**, **cadence (every_days, max_missed)**, **reinstruct (enabled, every_calls, every_seconds, max_items)**, **cadence again (integration_tests_every_tasks, architecture_review_every_phases, mutation_tests_every_phases, dedupe_sweep_every_tasks, lessons_pass_every_phases)**, rules, ci, … while the dataclasses are declared in the order … Companions, **Reinstruct, Cadence** … . The two `cadence` doc groups are split around all four `reinstruct` docs, and the `gates` docs sit before both. If each section module now calls `_doc` for its own knobs (which is what "with their … `_doc` knob-doc calls move verbatim to `config_sections/<section>.py`" describes), then importing the modules in declaration order emits all `cadence` docs contiguously and all `reinstruct` docs contiguously, i.e. `_doc("cadence","every_days")`/`max_missed` now land *after* the four `reinstruct` docs instead of before them, and the `gates` pair moves to wherever `GatesConfig` is declared. Because `KNOB_DOCS` insertion order *is* `ddflow config --explain` order, the explain output reorders for any project containing these knobs. The only way to keep the order unchanged is to leave every `_doc` call centralized in `_docs.py`, which contradicts the per-section-move description; the invariant claimed in the intent cannot be achieved by "import the sections in declaration order" alone.

chunk_findings.detail: `family_for` lowercases the model (`low = (model or "").lower()`) but compares the raw key (`if needle in low`). `FAMILY_HINTS` ships all-lowercase keys so the default path is unaffected, but the map is explicitly user-extensible ("Extend it as new families appear", and `families` is an env-overridable field). Given `families={"Claude": "anthropic"}` and `model="claude-3-5-sonnet"`, `low` is `"claude-3-5-sonnet"`, the needle `"Claude"` is not a substring, and the function returns `""` (unknown) instead of `"anthropic"`. The same input through `router_set` *would* match, because it lowercases the needle. This contradicts the "case-blind substring" contract stated in `router_set`'s docstring and silently changes independence classification for any project that writes its family keys with the model's display capitalization.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/agent.py:family_for

chunk_findings.detail: `family_for` also lacks the `needle and ...` guard that `router_set` deliberately applies, so an empty key matches every model. Given `families={"": "openai"}` (again an overridable map) and any model, e.g. `model="qwen2.5"`, `"" in "qwen2.5"` is `True` and the function returns `"openai"`, classifying every model — and therefore every reviewer — as OpenAI family. `router_set` guards against exactly this (`if not (needle and needle.lower() in low)`); `family_for` does not.

chunk_findings.detail:
The `_doc` registration order inside this section does not match the dataclass field-declaration order: `EnforceConfig` declares `stale_docs` (field 8) *before* `environment_commits` (field 9), but the two `_doc(...)` calls are emitted in the opposite sequence — `generated_views`, then `environment_commits`, then `stale_docs`. Per the stated design, `KNOB_DOCS` is built from `_doc` call order and drives `ddflow config --explain`, so the explain output for `[enforce]` now lists `environment_commits` ahead of `stale_docs`. In a truly verbatim move the `_doc` calls are expected to preserve the pre-move insertion order (which mirrors the field order in the class body); this adjacent swap of exactly one pair is the kind of change the refactor promised not to make, and anything that regressed-tests or diffs `--explain` output ordering will see the section reordered.

(If the pre-move `config.py` genuinely registered `environment_commits` before `stale_docs`, this is a no-op; but then field and doc order were already inconsistent, which the "verbatim move" claim should be checked against the deleted `config.py` text.)

chunk_findings.detail: The `_doc` calls for the `[loops]` section are emitted in a different order than the corresponding dataclass fields: `LoopsConfig` declares `max_reopens` (line 18) before `max_repeated_failures` (line 19), but the module registers the docs as `... max_repeated_failures ...` (the block starting at line 35) before `... max_reopens ...` (the block starting at line 40). `_doc` is what appends into `KNOB_DOCS`, and `config --explain` iterates `KNOB_DOCS` in insertion order, whereas the dataclass field order is what drives config serialization / positional construction. So the move silently reorders the explain output for these two knobs (and/or the serialized key order) relative to the original `config.py`, where the docs would have followed the field declaration order. This contradicts the stated invariant that `KNOB_DOCS` order (= `config --explain` order) is unchanged. If any test snapshots `config --explain` output, it will fail; if not, users see `max_repeated_failures` documented before `max_reopens` while the file/serialized config lists them in the opposite order.

chunk_findings.detail: The new filter `"config_sections" not in p.parts` tests every path component of the absolute `p` returned by `pkg.rglob("*.py")`, not just components relative to `pkg`. Because `pkg` is typically built from an absolute `__file__`, `p.parts` includes the full checkout path. If the repository is checked out under any ancestor directory literally named `config_sections` (for example `/tmp/config_sections/ddflow`), then every scanned file has `"config_sections"` in its `p.parts`, the generator drops all source files, the concatenated source is empty, and the dead-knob ratchet passes vacuously instead of checking for dead knobs. The exclusion should be based on the path relative to the package root (e.g. `p.relative_to(pkg).parts[0] != "config_sections"`) rather than on all absolute path components.

chunk_findings.detail:
The move relocates each section's `_doc(...)` calls into that section's own module (`config_sections/<section>.py`), so they now execute at section-import time and the insertion order of `KNOB_DOCS` becomes section-contiguous. But in the original `ddflow/config.py` the calls were deliberately *not* section-contiguous, and the removed hunk shows exactly where: `_doc("cadence", "every_days", …)` and `_doc("cadence", "max_missed", …)` were registered **before** the four `_doc("reinstruct", …)` entries, which were in turn registered **before** `_doc("cadence", "integration_tests_every_tasks", …)`, `architecture_review_every_phases`, `mutation_tests_every_phases`, `dedupe_sweep_every_tasks` and `lessons_pass_every_phases` (and the `_doc("gates", "rate_min_runs"…)` / `_doc("gates", "rate_max_fail"…)` pair sat between the companions docs and the cadence docs).

No import order of whole section modules can reproduce that interleaving: whichever of `cadence.py` / `reinstruct.py` `__init__` imports first, all five later `cadence` docs end up on the same side of the `reinstruct` block, so the relative order of `cadence.integration_tests_every_tasks` vs. `reinstruct.enabled` flips. Since `ddflow config --explain` iterates `KNOB_DOCS` (the change's stated invariant is that its order is unchanged), the same command now prints the reinstruct and the count-based cadence knobs in a different order than before, and any test that pins that order will fail. Input: `ddflow config --explain`; expected the original interleaved order, actual grouped-by-section order.

chunk_findings.detail: In this section the KNOB_DOCS registration order tracks the dataclass field order for every knob (commit_without_lease, install_hooks_on_setup, require_item_trailer, item_trailer_keys, forbidden_trailers, trailer_waivers, generated_views, doc_globs, doc_exclude, stale_rules, readme_with_code, readme_code_globs, readme_files, behind, max_behind), with exactly one inversion: `EnforceConfig` declares `stale_docs: str = "warn"` immediately before `environment_commits: str = "block"`, but the `_doc` calls register `environment_commits` before `stale_docs`. Since `KNOB_DOCS` order *is* `config --explain` order (the stated invariant of this refactor), `ddflow config --explain` will now print `enforce.environment_commits` ahead of `enforce.stale_docs`, which is a user-visible ordering change from the original `config.py` and will fail any golden/expected `--explain` output. If instead the dataclass field order was the thing that drifted during the move, the same swap surfaces through any code that serialises the dataclass (`dataclasses.asdict`, `config --init`, `repr`), which is likewise order-sensitive. A verbatim move cannot have produced both orders matching every other knob yet disagreeing on this one pair, so one of the two orders was altered.

chunk_findings.detail: When a `lease.released` event carries only `holder` (the documented legacy form), and that holder has an older claim still sitting in `it.lease_contest` while a newer claim of theirs is the displayed lease, the fold withdraws the *older* contested claim and returns before the common release path, so the holder's actual latest claim (the displayed lease) is never released. Concrete log: C acquires `e1` at t=100; H acquires `e2` at t=150 so the two intervals overlap (`_join` puts `e1` and `e2` in `it.lease_contest`, and `e2` is displayed); H re-acquires `e3` at t=300 — `_h_lease_acquired` sees `cur.holder == new.holder`, displaces `e2` (adding it to `it.displaced`) but leaves it in `lease_contest`, and displays `e3`; then a legacy `lease.released {"holder": "H"}` arrives. `_released_claim(it.displaced, d)` removes H's displaced `e2`, and `_released_claim(it.lease_contest, d)` returns H's latest *contested* claim, which is `e2`; `_withdraw_claim(it, e2)` runs and the handler returns. The displayed lease `e3` — H's latest claim, the one the release names by holder — stays live. This contradicts `_released_claim`'s stated contract ("it is taken to end that holder's LATEST claim -- the one it held when it released") and the handler's rule 1 ("a release only ends the lease it names"); it also skips the deliberate-release state transition (`it.state = OPEN`) performed only in the common path. Picking the holder's latest claim across `lease_contest ∪ displaced ∪ displayed` (or falling through to the common path when the contest match is not the displayed lease) is needed.
